headline: Where'd the bass go at noon? Ask the neap tide and the bridge lights
subhead: Daytime stripers have gone underground with the mid-70s water, but the fluke are peaking and the triggerfish are finally showing on the wrecks.
body_markdown:
I get this question every August, and I got it three times at the ramp this week: "I fished Absecon Inlet at one in the afternoon and never had a sniff — what happened to the bass?" Class, this is the easiest lesson on the syllabus. Water's sitting in the mid-70s off the beachfront, low 70s in the back bay channels, and a striper's metabolism doesn't love that. They're not gone. They're down deep on structure — the Route 30 bridge pilings, the rock piles at the base of Absecon Inlet, the Ocean City bridge abutments — sitting tight to shade and current until the sun drops. Come dusk, dark, and the early flood, they climb up and feed. That's the whole pattern right now, and it's not going to change until the water cools.

We flagged this shift last week, and it's playing out exactly as expected — as the tides soften into this weekend's neap (bottoming out around August 5-6), the current at the inlets gets lazier, and that pushes bass into the strongest hours of moving water and the deepest, coolest structure they can find. Night eels — the classic 6- to 9-inch rigged eel, or a black/purple Slug-Go on a jighead — fished slow along the bridge lights at Absecon and the Ninth Street bridge in Ocean City has been the play after 9 p.m., outgoing tide especially. Daytime, if you insist on trying, drop bucktails or jig a soft plastic tight to the Great Egg rock jetty on the bottom third of the tide. Don't expect much before last light.

Now the fluke — this is where I'd spend my daylight hours, because the program is as good as it's been all season. Doormat-class fish are showing on ocean-side structure and inlet rips from Absecon down through Great Egg, and the back bay sod banks are holding steady numbers too. My best fish this week came off the edge of the Great Egg reef in 22 to 28 feet, drifting white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails with the outgoing tide pulling hard — a 5-pounder and two keepers in the 19- to 21-inch range in about ninety minutes. In the back bay, the Rainbow Channel edges and the sod banks off Bader Field are still stacking shorts with enough keepers mixed in to make it worth the gas, minnow-and-Gulp combo on a light egg sinker, fished slow on the last two hours of the outgoing when the bait gets flushed off the flats. Townsends Inlet and the Sea Isle side channels are producing the same way — nothing easy, but steady if you keep the boat moving and cover water.

Bluefish are the wild card. The bunker-driven blitz that's been tearing up the beachfront from Belmar south hasn't fully arrived here yet, but I wouldn't sleep on it — bunker schools have been pushing south along the coast, and this fishery is entirely bait-driven. Wherever those pods settle, blues show up within hours. Keep an eye on the surf off Ocean City and Brigantine for diving birds and nervous water; if the bunker set up tight to the beach, bring a metal-lipped swimmer or a diamond jig and don't wait around, because these blitzes come and go fast.

Here's a bright spot that's new for the season: triggerfish. We noted a couple weeks back that the first ones were showing on the inshore pieces, and sure enough they're building now on the wrecks and rock piles off Absecon and Great Egg as the water's peaked into the high 70s nearshore. Small pieces of clam or squid on a light fluke rig, fished right on the structure, has been drawing strikes from anglers who know to look for them — most are still on the smaller side, but a few keeper-class fish are mixed in. If you've got a wreck number in that 40- to 60-foot range off the reef sites, it's worth a stop on your way out or back.

Surf-wise, kingfish are still working the wash from Ocean City down to Stone Harbor on bloodworm and Fishbites rigs, small stuff but a fun way to fill a bucket on a calm morning tide. And offshore, the settled high-pressure pattern has kept the mako and thresher fleet busy running out of Absecon Inlet — not my program, but it tells you the ocean's been flat and cooperative, which is exactly why the inshore bite has been so structure-dependent this week. No wind to stir up bait, no current to push fish around — they're sitting right where the temperature and tide put them.

Looking ahead: as this neap tide bottoms out this weekend, expect the bass bite to compress even further into that narrow night window at the bridges and inlets — lighter jigs, slower retrieves, patience over volume. Fluke should hold strong through the coming week since the water's stable and the bait's still moving on the tide. And if that bunker pod finally slides south past Long Beach Island, watch for the blitz to show on the Ocean City and Brigantine beachfront within a few days of it arriving — that's a fast-developing pattern, so if you hear about it, don't wait for the weekend.
